# Problem 10.62: a periodic group generated by odd transpositions

Date: 11 September 2026.
Status: candidate resolution, subject to outside review and novelty checks.
The geometric existence theorem is imported from Amelio 2025, as specified
below; the application and the deductions are proved here.

## Result

For every sufficiently large odd prime p there is an infinite, three-generated
perfect group G of exponent 2p with no subgroup of order four. Its involutions
form one conjugacy class X, generate G, and satisfy

    |xy| = p  for all distinct x,y in X.

Consequently G has no subgroup of index two. This supplies the periodic
example requested in Problem 10.62 of the supplied Notebook, printed page 43.
The condition also holds when the two involutions are equal: their product
has order one, which is odd.

No explicit numerical threshold for p is claimed. The construction is an
infinite sequence of small cancellation quotients, not a finite presentation
or a finite computation. No assertion of simplicity is needed or made.

## 1. The precise geometric input

Our source is Marco Amelio, *Non-split sharply 2-transitive groups of bounded
exponent*, [arXiv:2509.11958v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11958v2), submitted
16 September 2025. The PDF itself is dated 17 September 2025. All references
below use v2 and its printed page numbers. The relevant statements were
compared with the PDF images, not just the extracted text.

We use Theorem 6.7, pp.40–42, together with the construction in its proof,
Proposition 6.1, pp.36–39, and Remark 6.8, p.42. The following are the features
of that construction needed here.

Let a group F act acylindrically and non-elementarily on a hyperbolic length
space T. Assume the action is **tame**, meaning that F has no subgroup of
order four and the maximal finite normal subgroup of each maximal
loxodromic subgroup has order at most two (Definition 4.46). Assume also
that the parameters tau and Omega are finite and the injectivity radius is
positive. Taking Q to be all loxodromic elements is permitted by Remark 6.6.

For any sufficiently large odd integer p, the construction with exponent
family {p} gives a sequence of epimorphisms

    F = F_0 -> F_1 -> F_2 -> ... -> G.

It has these properties:

1. Elliptic subgroups of F embed in G; G is infinite.
2. The image of every loxodromic element of F either has order dividing 2p
   or is the image of an elliptic element of F.
3. Every F_i has a tame action, in particular no subgroup of order four.
4. After an admissible initial rescaling, the first step kills the p-th
   powers of a maximal family of pairwise inequivalent primitive
   loxodromic elements of length at most L_S delta_1. An eligible prescribed
   primitive element can be included in that family.

Items 1–2 are conclusions of Theorem 6.7. Item 3 comes from Proposition 6.1
at every step; the preservation of tameness is Proposition 5.36, p.35.
Item 4 is the explicit definition of F_1 in Proposition 6.1 and in the
proof of Theorem 6.7, p.41. Remark 6.8 expressly permits making the initial
scale smaller, at the cost of increasing the lower bound on the odd
exponents. Thus item 4 is not being inferred from the headline conclusions
of Theorem 6.7 alone.

The geometric proofs underlying Proposition 6.1 are imported. In particular,
we do not claim to have independently reproved the hyperbolic cone-off and
small cancellation theorems on which it depends. The reading and dependency
audit is in `10.62-review.md`.

## 2. A concrete initial action

Put

    F = <a,b,c | a^2=b^2=c^2=1> = C2 * C2 * C2.

Use its Cayley graph for the generating set {a,b,c}, with edges of length
one, viewed as a metric tree T. Vertices are reduced words, and multiplying
on the right by a generator appends that letter or cancels the final equal
letter. Each edge is labeled by its generator. Left multiplication by F
preserves the tree and the edge labels.

Vertices have trivial stabilizers. The midpoint of an edge can have a
stabilizer of order two, generated by the element exchanging its endpoints;
every other point has trivial stabilizer. In particular each nontrivial
elliptic element is an involution fixing exactly one edge midpoint.

A finite subgroup fixes a point of this metric tree: take the center of
the finite subtree spanned by a finite orbit. It therefore has order at
most two. This proves, in particular, the required absence of subgroups of
order four in F.

The action is acylindrical. More strongly, for each R the number of group
elements moving any specified point a distance at most R is bounded
independently of the point. Choose a vertex within distance 1/2 of that
point. Such an element moves this vertex at most R+1, and the trivalent
tree has a uniform finite bound on the size of that ball; vertex
stabilizers are trivial. This implies the two-point condition defining
acylindricity. The same uniform bound shows that every elliptic subgroup
is finite: a bounded orbit bounds all its elements' displacements at one
point. Such a subgroup therefore has order at most two as proved above.

The action is non-elementary. For example ab and ac are translations whose
axes have different pairs of endpoints at infinity. A reduced word with
cyclically reduced length at least two translates along an axis by that
length. All other elements are conjugate to 1,a,b, or c. Thus every element
is either elliptic of order at most two or loxodromic, and

    r_inj(F,T) = 2 > 0.

To check the remaining tameness condition, let E be a maximal loxodromic
subgroup and let A be its invariant axis. The action of E on A has trivial
kernel, because A contains vertices and their stabilizers in F are trivial.
Its image is an infinite subgroup of the isometry group of a simplicial
line, hence is infinite cyclic or infinite dihedral. Neither of these has
a nontrivial finite normal subgroup. The required finite kernel is
therefore trivial, a stronger assertion than tameness requires.

We also check the parameters, rather than assuming finiteness implicitly.
The parameter nu from Definition 4.43 is at most one. Indeed, if h is
loxodromic and <g,h^(-1)gh> is elliptic, that subgroup has order at most two.
If g were nontrivial, h^(-1)gh=g, so h would preserve the unique fixed point
of g, contradicting that h is loxodromic. Thus g=1, and <g,h> is elementary.
It follows that tau=max{nu,3}=3.

For precision with the strict inequalities in Definition 4.28, regard T as
delta-hyperbolic for a fixed positive

    delta < min{1/L_S, 1/100}.

Then Omega in Definition 4.51 is zero. Every element occurring in its
defining tuples has translation length at most L_S delta<1, hence is
elliptic. For a nonidentity such element g, let v be its unique fixed edge
midpoint. The displacement formula d(x,gx)=2d(x,v) shows that A_g from
Definition 4.28 is the open ball of radius 4 delta about v. Its
13 delta-neighborhood lies within radius 17 delta of v. Distinct fixed
edge midpoints have distance at least one; these neighborhoods are
therefore disjoint for distinct nontrivial elliptic elements. A tuple
generating a non-elementary subgroup must contain two such elements.
Its overlap diameter is consequently zero, under the convention for empty
intersections used in these nonnegative overlap parameters. Thus Omega=0.
Using positive delta also avoids any degenerate interpretation of A_g when
delta=0; no zero-hyperbolicity limit is needed.

Finally Q, the set of all loxodromic elements, is conjugation invariant and
strongly stable as required, by Remark 6.6. No condition on a subgroup
generated by translations is imposed in this theorem.

## 3. Choosing an odd relation at the first step

Let w=abc. It has cyclically reduced length three and acts by translation
of length three. We verify that it is primitive in precisely the geometric
sense needed in Proposition 6.1.

Its axis through the identity has the bi-infinite periodic edge-label
pattern abcabcabc..., read in the direction of w. Any orientation-preserving
element stabilizing this axis preserves its labels. The smallest positive
shift preserving the pattern has length three. The action on vertices is
free, so the orientation-preserving stabilizer is exactly <w>.

There is no orientation-reversing element in the stabilizer. Such an
element would identify the pattern abc with its reverse cba up to cyclic
shift, but cba is none of abc,bca,cab. Equivalently, a reflection at an edge
midpoint would exchange two differently labeled adjacent edges; a
reflection at a vertex is already excluded by its trivial stabilizer.
Consequently the maximal loxodromic subgroup containing w is precisely
<w>, and w is a primitive generator.

Let L_S and delta_1 be the positive constants of Proposition 6.1. Choose
the initial rescaling lambda>0 sufficiently small that

    3 lambda <= L_S delta_1,

in addition to the initialization requirements in the proof of Theorem 6.7,
including lambda delta<=delta_1.
This is allowed by Remark 6.8. The rescaled injectivity radius is still
positive, namely 2 lambda. Increasing the critical exponent compensates
for its reduction: the lower bound on that radius in Proposition 6.1 is a
constant times n_1^(-1/2), and the contraction constant also decreases as
n_1 increases. The tau and Omega bounds stay valid under this rescaling.

Fix any odd prime p above the resulting critical exponent, with p>3. Take
the exponent family to be {p}. In the first maximal selection P_0 in the
proof of Theorem 6.7 include w. This is possible because it is eligible;
extend the singleton {w} to a maximal selection, for example by enumerating
the countable set of eligible elements and adding compatible ones. The
equivalence relation is the one specified in Proposition 6.1. There is no
prescribed selection that forces w to be omitted.

The first quotient is by the normal closure of the p-th powers of the
selected elements. Therefore

    w^p = (abc)^p = 1 in F_1 and hence in G.                 (1)

One could equivalently choose any representative of w's equivalence class:
because its maximal loxodromic group is <w>, that representative is conjugate
to w or w^(-1), giving the same normal closure. We use the explicit choice
to avoid any dependence on that reformulation.

The constants and this fixed scaling are chosen before p. Thus the argument
works for every sufficiently large odd prime, without the restriction
p=3 mod 4 occurring in the sharply 2-transitive application of the paper.
Our initial group contains no AGL(1,F_p) subgroup and needs no WST hypothesis.

## 4. Properties of the limit

Denote the images of a,b,c in G by the same letters. They are involutions,
not identities: their cyclic subgroups are elliptic in F and embed by
Theorem 6.7(1). They generate G since every map in the construction is onto.
Theorem 6.7(4) states that G is infinite. It is countable as a quotient of F.

Every element of F is elliptic or belongs to Q. Its image therefore has
order dividing 2p, by Theorem 6.7(3) and the order bound on elliptic
elements of F. Thus G is periodic of exponent dividing 2p.

We must justify separately that the absence of order-four subgroups passes
to the limit; merely quoting the conclusion of Theorem 6.7 would not suffice.

**Finite-subgroup limit lemma.** If H is a finite subgroup of the direct
limit of a sequence of epimorphisms F_i, then H embeds in some F_j.

Choose a lift in F_0 of each element h in H, with 1 lifted to 1. There are
finitely many multiplication identities among these chosen lifts. Each
identity that holds in the limit holds in a sufficiently late F_j; choose
one j for all of them. The lifts then define a homomorphism H->F_j. Its
composition with F_j->G is the given inclusion H->G, so it is injective.
This proves the lemma.

Each F_j has no subgroup of order four by the tame conclusion of
Proposition 6.1. The lemma therefore implies

    G has no subgroup isomorphic to C4 or C2 x C2.          (2)

## 5. Products and conjugacy of involutions

Here is the elementary implication that converts (2) into the requested
condition. Let x,y be distinct involutions in a group of exponent dividing
2p and having no subgroup of order four. Put t=xy. The order of t is a
nontrivial divisor of 2p.

Suppose its order d is even. The element z=t^(d/2) is an involution.
Conjugation by x inverts t, and hence fixes z. Also x is not in <t>.
Indeed, if x belonged to <t>, then y=xt would too; a cyclic group has at most
one involution, contrary to x!=y. Thus x and z are distinct commuting
involutions, giving a subgroup C2 x C2, a contradiction. It follows that

    |xy|=p.                                               (3)

This argument applies to **all** involutions in G, including any that arise
in the limit. It does not require a theorem that every involution lifts to
an involution in the original free product.

Equation (3) also proves conjugacy within G. If t=xy has odd order p and
k=(p+1)/2, then

    t^(-k) x t^k = x t^(2k) = xt = y.

Thus all involutions form a single conjugacy class X. The group is
generated by X, since a,b,c belong to X and already generate it.

There must be at least two distinct involutions. Otherwise a=b=c and G
would be cyclic of order two, contradicting (1) for odd p (or infinitude).
Together with (3) and the existence of involutions this proves that the
exponent of G is exactly 2p, not merely a divisor of it.

## 6. No subgroup of index two; in fact G is perfect

Let phi:G->C2 be any homomorphism, writing C2 additively. All involutions
are conjugate, so phi(a)=phi(b)=phi(c)=epsilon. Relation (1) implies

    0 = phi((abc)^p) = 3p epsilon = epsilon.

Since a,b,c generate G, phi is trivial. Every subgroup of index two is
normal and gives a nontrivial quotient map to C2. Hence there is no such
subgroup in G.

More generally the abelianization is generated by three elements of order
dividing two. Conjugacy makes all three equal, and (1) kills their common
image. Thus G_ab=1. This proves the stated perfectness as well.

The requested periodic construction is complete relative to the explicitly
imported geometric theorem and its audited construction features.

## 7. Scope, attribution, and controls

The existence engine, its tameness preservation, and its adjustable initial
scale are Amelio's prior work. The proposed contribution here is their
application to the three-involution free product with the selected odd
relation, giving the exact conclusion of Problem 10.62. The supplied
Notebook leaves 10.62 unmarked while marking adjacent 10.64 solved by this
same paper. This is evidence about the supplied problem list, not proof of
novelty. The candidate requires further priority review.

The older Amelio--Andre--Tent construction explicitly excludes involutions
from the subgroup generated by translations. Taking that older
involution-generated subgroup would leave an index-two subgroup and would
not prove our claim. Amelio's Remark 2.12 distinguishes the new framework.

The finite controls in `scripts/verify_10_62.g` check the dihedral conjugator,
the order-four obstruction, and the effect of the odd relation on
abelianization. They do not construct G or certify the imported geometric
theorem. No finite GAP output is used as evidence of the infinitude of G.
